sm: Ben Shapiro lists a week of breakdowns, including Microsoft Outlook and Teams, the FAA, Workday, major banks, United Airlines, the National Weather Service and the NSA. He says distrust of institutions is already high, so people feel panic when technology stops working, and that officials are communicating poorly. He cites a Wall Street Journal piece describing relentless AI-driven cyber attacks, a flood of software patches, and an AI hacking tool called Xbow. Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI models are finding bugs at record rates, and Microsoft patched about 1400 flaws in one month versus 170 a year earlier. He argues that rapid, simultaneous updates bring bugs, but that bugs are now fixed faster than at any time in tech history.

Shapiro walks through the timeline: a 24-hour Microsoft outage affecting some 430 million people, a five-hour FAA ground stop traced to a contractor replacing copper wiring with fiber, a Workday outage, bank disruptions, a two-hour United outage, a National Weather Service disruption, an Apple update problem and degraded NSA internal systems. He says new technology adopted at scale exposes bugs at scale. He faults the government for lacking transparency, because without clear explanations people assume incompetence or malice. He plays Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin saying there is no attack, notes an FBI flash advisory about AI-powered hacking, and plays Marco Rubio dismissing leaked threat reports. He says CNN found no public evidence of hostile attacks, and plays JD Vance saying Americans need not build bunkers.

Shapiro notes that Vance abruptly canceled a DealBook Summit appearance, which fueled unease, and that mystery is not helpful. He cites a Google report that hackers use AI models to scan updates and exploit fixes before teams can apply them, and plays a commentator blaming superintelligence for the outages. He then asks who can fix the problem, arguing the government cannot. Congress understands little about AI, politicians have an incentive to overreact and shift blame, and the government has not fixed FAA wiring in twenty years. He says private companies like Microsoft, airlines and banks have a strong incentive to fix failures quickly because markets punish failure. He adds that tech leaders are a constantly shifting group, and that Silicon Valley's strange behavior hurts public trust in markets.

Shapiro reads a Washington Free Beacon report that an Anthropic cybersecurity researcher manages a company hosting orgies in the Bay Area, which have drawn sexual assault allegations. He says such morality need not win out, since companies that do poorly get replaced, and he rejects both government control and close government-tech partnership. He turns to Nvidia, saying the scandal is that Jensen Huang allegedly used government connections to open a loophole sending chips to China. Huang tweeted that he would return as CEO if the board wished, but interim CEO Colette Kress said the board will not reinstate him.

Shapiro reads the Commerce Department and Justice Department statement on the investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore firm led by Huang's alleged Chinese spy partner. He says Huang and Nvidia agreed to appear before Congress and the SEC opened a civil probe. Nvidia's loans to data center companies grew by nearly 140 billion dollars last quarter, which may have worried the board. He argues business should not be intertwined with government and plays Jeff Bezos praising Trump's accessibility. He cites a CNN poll showing only 26 percent approve of Trump's handling of AI, and says the left will use the chaos to attack the industry, quoting Mehdi Hasan and Greta Thunberg on overthrowing capitalism.

Shapiro says that when Democrats run things the results show in California. Gavin Newsom urges party unity, while a landfill near Los Angeles erupted in a 500-foot geyser of trash and methane. He cites fraud cases involving a Long Beach housing charity CEO caught with cash, a nonprofit founder charged with siphoning 7.5 million dollars, and a homeless services authority giving up control of 150 million dollars in federal funds. He plays Newsom criticizing Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. He then covers Trump's meetings in China with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, internal fights over chips and China policy, Taiwan, and the Iran blockade. He plays Senator Tom Cotton calling for a victory strategy and Tucker Carlson saying Trump wants to de-escalate.

Shapiro says Democrats are moving too far left. He covers New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani touting over 500 million dollars from a tax on second homes worth over five million, while the city will mail bills to only about 7,500 owners, and Ken Griffin selling his Park Avenue duplex. He says Mamdani's disbanding of the police Strategic Response Group creates a rioter's veto, and plays Mamdani defending a civilian de-escalation approach. He then covers Ayanna Pressley's priorities, including reparations, Medicare for all, abolishing ICE and stopping data centers, which he says would raise costs. He notes Hakeem Jeffries won the House Democratic leadership vote 251 to 11, and says woke politics is returning under a new name.
sg: Tech Excess and the Nvidia Scandal
